questions.q: Why does this course measure algorithms by counting steps instead of timing them with a clock?
questions.explain: performance.now() is precise, but what it measures mixes your algorithm with everything else happening on the machine. A step count isolates the algorithm, so it gives the same answer everywhere. You still confirm with a clock, carefully, at realistic sizes.
options: Clocks in JavaScript are not precise enough to measure anything under a second
The step count depends only on the algorithm and the input; the time also depends on the machine, other programs, the JIT and the garbage collector
Counting steps is always faster than running the code
Timings are forbidden in production code

questions.q: A function does exactly 4n² + 100n + 7 steps. What is its time complexity?
questions.explain: Drop the lower-order terms (100n + 7) and the constant factor (4). For large n the n² term dominates everything. O(n³) is technically a true upper bound, but not the tight one you should state.
options: O(n²)
O(n³)

questions.q: Function A does 2n steps and function B does 50n steps. Which statement is correct?
questions.explain: Big O describes the shape of the growth, not the speed. Both grow linearly. The constant factor is real (B is 25 times slower) but it does not change the class. That is why Big O alone cannot pick between two algorithms of the same class.
options: A is O(n) and B is O(n²), because 50 is much larger than 2
Both are O(n): doubling n doubles the work of each, although B is 25 times slower at every size
Both are O(1), because the constants are fixed
They cannot be compared with Big O

questions.q: A report function loops over all n orders to compute the total, then loops over them again to find the largest order. What is its time complexity?
questions.explain: Sequential blocks add: n + n = 2n, which is O(n). Only nested loops multiply.
options: O(n)
O(n²)
O(2ⁿ)
O(log n)

questions.q: For every one of n orders, a function scans all m products. How should you state its time complexity?
questions.explain: Nested loops multiply, and different inputs keep different letters. Calling it O(n²) hides the fact that the two sizes can be very different: 100,000 orders times 20 products is far cheaper than 100,000 times 100,000.
options: O(n²)
O(n + m)
O(n · m)
O(n), because products do not count

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this loop, where n is the starting balance?
questions.explain: The value halves on every pass, so the loop runs about log₂ n times. A loop variable that is multiplied or divided gives a logarithm; one that goes up or down by a constant gives a linear loop.
options: O(n)
O(log n)

questions.q: What does "the running time is Ω(n)" say?
questions.explain: Ω (omega) is a lower bound, O an upper bound, and Θ (theta) both at once: a tight bound. "Exactly n steps" would be Θ(n), and only if it held for every n from some point on.
options: The running time grows no faster than n
The running time grows at least as fast as n (a lower bound)
The running time is exactly n steps
The running time is the average over all inputs

questions.q: Which function is Θ(n) for every input of size n?
questions.explain: Summing visits every item exactly once, whatever the values, so it is always linear: a tight Θ(n). The search that stops early is Θ(1) in its best case and Θ(n) in its worst case, so no single Θ covers all its inputs.
options: Finding an order by ID with a loop that stops at the first match
Summing every price in a cart
Binary search in a sorted list
Reading the first item of an array

questions.q: A teammate says "Big O means the worst case". What is the accurate version?
questions.explain: "Worst case O(n)" combines two ideas: which inputs (the worst ones) and which bound (an upper bound). You can also say "best case Θ(1)" or "worst case Ω(n)". Mixing them up leads to wrong claims such as "the best case is Ω".
options: They are right: Big O, Ω and Θ are the worst, best and average case
Big O is an upper bound on a function; best, worst and average case are different functions of n, and each can be described with O, Ω or Θ
Big O means the average case; worst case is written W(n)
Big O only applies to sorting algorithms

questions.q: A login service looks users up with a function whose average case is fast and whose worst case is slow. Why do engineers usually plan around the worst case?
questions.explain: An average depends on an assumption about which inputs arrive. An attacker does not follow your assumption. Planning for the worst case (or limiting who can trigger it) keeps the service up under hostile input.
options: Because the average case is impossible to compute
The worst case is a promise that holds for every input, and in a backend some inputs come from people who can choose slow ones on purpose
Because the best case is always equal to the worst case
Because Big O only describes the worst case

questions.q: Linear search over n orders takes (n + 1) / 2 comparisons on average when every order is equally likely. What is the average case complexity?
questions.explain: Dividing by a constant (2) does not change the class. Doubling the list still doubles the average work. "Halving the work once" is very different from "halving what is left at every step", which is what gives O(log n).
options: O(1), because it usually stops halfway
O(log n), because it halves the work
O(n): half of n is still linear
O(n²)

questions.q: A print server empties its queue like this. What is the total time for n jobs?
questions.explain: Removing the first array item is O(n) because the other items move. n shifts cost about n²/2 moves. The lesson on stacks and queues builds a queue that removes from the front in O(1).
options: O(n): one shift per job
O(n²): each shift moves every remaining job one place forward
O(log n)
O(1) per job, O(1) total

questions.q: orders.filter((o) => vipIds.includes(o.customerId)) is slow with 100,000 orders and 5,000 VIPs. What is the best fix?
questions.explain: includes is a scan, so it runs m steps for each of n orders. A Set lookup is O(1) on average. A plain for loop or indexOf still scans.
options: Replace filter with a for loop
Sort orders first
Build const vips = new Set(vipIds) once and use vips.has(o.customerId), turning O(n · m) into O(n + m)
Use indexOf instead of includes

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this function for n orders?
questions.explain: Spread is a loop. On the k-th order it copies k - 1 ids, so the total is 0 + 1 + … + (n - 1), about n²/2. orders.map((o) => o.id) or a push loop is O(n).
options: O(n): reduce visits each order once
O(n²): each step copies the whole array built so far
O(n log n)

questions.q: What does "push is amortized O(1)" mean?
questions.explain: Amortized cost averages over a sequence of operations, not over inputs. Because the array grows by a constant factor, the expensive copies are rare enough that their total stays proportional to n.
options: Every single push takes the same constant time
Push is O(1) on average over random inputs
A single push may cost O(n) when the array must grow, but any sequence of n pushes costs O(n) in total, so O(1) per push
Push is O(1) only when the array is empty

questions.q: A custom list grows its capacity by 100 slots whenever it is full. What is the total cost of n pushes?
questions.explain: Growing by a constant amount gives about n / 100 copies of sizes 100, 200, 300, …, which sum to about n² / 200. Only growing by a constant factor (2, 1.5) keeps the total linear.
options: O(n), the same as doubling
O(n²): it copies every 100 pushes, and each copy is proportional to the current size
O(n log n)

questions.q: What is the extra space used by this function for an array of n amounts?
questions.explain: Every unfinished call keeps a stack frame. The chain is n + 1 calls deep, so the space is O(n), and a large enough n throws "Maximum call stack size exceeded". A loop does the same sum in O(1) extra space.
options: O(1): it creates no arrays
O(n): up to n calls wait on the call stack at once
O(log n)
O(n²)

questions.q: Reversing an array in place by swapping from both ends uses how much extra space?
questions.explain: Extra (auxiliary) space counts memory beyond the input. The swaps reuse the input's own slots. The number of swaps is about time, not space.
options: O(1): only two indexes, whatever the length
O(n): the reversed array
O(n / 2): one swap per pair
O(log n)

questions.q: For a list of 8 items, an O(n²) function runs faster than an O(n log n) one. How is that possible?
questions.explain: Big O describes growth for large n. A simple quadratic loop with tiny constants can win for a handful of items, which is why many sort implementations use a simple quadratic sort for small pieces.
options: It is not possible; the measurement must be wrong
Big O ignores constant factors and setup costs; for small n those can dominate
For small inputs, O(n²) becomes O(1)
JavaScript turns quadratic loops into linear ones

questions.q: Which way of timing two algorithms gives a trustworthy conclusion?
questions.explain: Warm-up lets the JIT compile, the best of several runs removes noise, and the doubling ratio reveals the growth class. Tiny inputs hide the growth, and single timings change on every run.
options: Run each once on 10 items and compare the milliseconds
Run each once on a large input and print the milliseconds in a test
Warm each up, take the best of several runs, use realistic input sizes, and compare how the time changes when n doubles
Time only the faster one, because the slower one is obviously slower

questions.q: You double n and the step count goes from 10,240 to 22,528 (about ×2.2). Which class fits best?
questions.explain: Linear gives exactly ×2 and quadratic ×4. Slightly more than ×2 is the signature of n log n: the n doubles and the log n grows by one. Exponential would square the count, not multiply it by a small number.
options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(2ⁿ)

questions.q: Trying every combination of n coupons takes 2ⁿ steps. The checkout handles 20 coupons in a moment. What happens with 30?
questions.explain: Ten more coupons means ten more doublings. Exponential algorithms are only usable for small n; the course's backtracking and dynamic programming lessons show how to prune or reuse work.
options: It takes 1.5 times as long
It takes 10 times as long
It takes about 1,000 times as long, because each extra coupon doubles the work (2¹⁰ = 1,024)
It takes the same time, because the coupons are small

questions.q: An endpoint loops over 200 orders and runs one database query per order to load its customer. In Big O it is O(n). Why is it still a production problem?
questions.explain: This is the "N + 1 queries" problem. The model counts every step as equal, but I/O is thousands of times slower than a comparison. Load all 200 customers in one query instead.
options: Because O(n) is always too slow for web requests
Each query is a network round trip that costs as much as millions of in-memory steps; count round trips separately from CPU steps
Because databases are O(n²)
It is not a problem, since Big O says it is linear
Because loops cannot contain await

questions.q: Why does the lesson test the growth rate with step counters instead of timings?
questions.explain: A timing-based test fails when the machine is busy. An exact step count only changes when the algorithm changes, which is precisely what the test should catch.
options: Step counters make the code faster
Step counts are exact and repeatable, so an assertion such as "doubling n doubles the steps" never fails at random
Test runners cannot call performance.now()
Timings are always wrong

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The inner loop runs 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 times: 10 pairs, which is n(n - 1) / 2 for n = 5. Still O(n²): the constant ½ is dropped.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 1000 → 500 → 250 → 125 → 62 → 31 → 15 → 7 → 3 → 1: nine halvings. log₂ 1000 is about 9.97, and rounding down in each step makes it 9.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The inner loop runs 0 + 1 + … + (n - 1) times: 15 for 6 and 66 for 12. Doubling n multiplied the steps by 4.4, close to the ×4 of O(n²).

questions.q: A list starts with capacity 1 and doubles when full, copying every item into the new block. What does this print?
questions.explain: It grows when full at lengths 1, 2, 4 and 8, copying 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 items. The total copies stay below the final size times 2, which is why push is amortized O(1).

questions.q: Now the list grows by one slot at a time. What does this print?
questions.explain: Every push after the first copies everything: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15. That is n(n - 1) / 2, quadratic in total.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Finding each order costs 1, 2, 3 and 4 comparisons: 10 in total, 2.5 on average. That is (n + 1) / 2, still linear.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each call makes two more until n < 2, so the call tree grows exponentially: 15 calls for fib(5), over a million for fib(30). Dynamic programming removes the repeated calls.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every coupon is either in or out: 2³ = 8 combinations, including the empty one. Each extra coupon doubles the list.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Sequential loops add (4 + 4), nested loops multiply (4 × 4). The first is O(n), the second O(n²).

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: i takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64: seven passes, then 128 stops the loop. A loop variable that doubles runs O(log n) times.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each step copies what was collected so far: 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. For n items that is about n²/2: a hidden quadratic.

questions.q: Finish hasDuplicate(ids) in O(n) time using a Set. It must return true as soon as it sees an ID for the second time.
questions.explain: One pass with O(1) average has and add gives O(n) time and O(n) extra space. new Set(ids).size !== ids.length is also O(n), but it always processes the whole list instead of stopping at the first duplicate.

questions.q: Add a step counter to cheaperPairs: increase counter.steps once per comparison in the inner loop. The program then prints the steps for 10 and 20 prices, which shows the ×4 of O(n²).
questions.explain: The comparison runs n × n times. Doubling n from 10 to 20 multiplies the steps by 4: the signature of quadratic growth.

questions.q: Write returning(january, february) that returns the customers who appear in both lists, in January's order, in O(n + m) time.
questions.explain: Building the Set is O(m), and each of the n lookups is O(1) on average. Using february.includes inside the filter would be O(n · m).

questions.q: Finish push so the list doubles its capacity when full and counts every item it copies. After 100 pushes the program should print the number of copies and the capacity.
questions.explain: The list grows at 1, 2, 4, …, 64 items and copies 1 + 2 + … + 64 = 127 of them: fewer than two copies per push. That bounded total is what "amortized O(1)" means.

questions.q: Write reverseInPlace(items) that reverses the array using O(1) extra space (no new array) and returns it.
questions.explain: Two indexes walk towards each other and swap. The middle item of an odd-length array stays where it is, because the loop stops when left meets right. Time O(n), extra space O(1).

questions.q: The recursive sum overflows the call stack on 200,000 amounts. Rewrite it as a loop with O(1) extra space.
questions.explain: The recursion needs one stack frame per amount: O(n) space. The loop keeps only total: O(1) extra space, and no stack limit.

questions.q: Write growth(fn): it counts the steps of fn for n = 500 and n = 1000 and returns the ratio as a string with two decimals. Use it to show that linear is ×2 and pairs is about ×4.
questions.explain: The exact ratio for pairs is 499500 / 124750 = 4.004, which rounds to 4.00. Ratios of step counts are exact and repeatable, so they make good test assertions, unlike timings.

questions.q: The slow vipOrders (shown in the comment) is O(n · m) because of includes. Write an O(n + m) version that returns the same count.
questions.explain: Build the Set once (O(m)), then each lookup is O(1) on average. Building it inside the filter callback would rebuild it for every order and be even slower than the original.
